title: What if you drove to the Moon? #shorts
description:
What if you could drive to the Moon? At 100 km/h without stopping, the trip is about 160 days. A passenger jet would take about 18 days. Apollo 11 took roughly three days to reach lunar orbit.

Numbers: average Earth-Moon distance 384,400 km; time = distance / speed (384,400 / 100 = 3,844 hours = 160.2 days; at 120 km/h = 133.5 days; at 900 km/h = 17.8 days). Fuel estimate assumes a car using 7 litres per 100 km (384,400 km x 0.07 = about 26,900 litres) and ignores that no real car could make the trip.

Sources:
- Average lunar distance: NASA
- Apollo 11 transit time to lunar orbit, about three days: NASA and Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

Narration is a synthetic (AI-generated) voice. Visuals are original animated graphics.

scenes.say: The Moon is, on average, three hundred and eighty-four thousand, four hundred kilometres away.
At one hundred kilometres per hour, without ever stopping, that is one hundred and sixty days.
At one hundred and twenty, about one hundred and thirty-three. In a jet at nine hundred, about eighteen.
A typical car using seven litres per hundred kilometres would burn roughly twenty-seven thousand litres of fuel on the way.
Apollo astronauts needed roughly three days to reach lunar orbit.
So the Moon is a short trip for a rocket, and an impossible commute for a car.

show.text: A short trip for a rocket. An *impossible* commute for a car.
